reason: While the narrative clearly portrays the people as sinful and corrupt (explicitly stated as 'שִׁחֵ֣ת עַמְּךָ֔' - the people have corrupted themselves), the text does not present leaders as righteous. Aaron, the key leader present, actively and willingly participates in crafting the golden calf. He doesn't resist the people's demands; instead, he collects their gold and fashions the idol himself ('וַיִּקַּ֣ח מִיָּדָ֗ם וַיָּ֤צַר אֹתוֹ֙ בַּחֶ֔רֶט'). When confronted, Aaron deflects blame rather than taking responsibility ('אַתָּה֙ יָדַ֣עְתָּ אֶת־הָעָ֔ם כִּ֥י בְרָ֖ע הֽוּא'). While Moses demonstrates righteous leadership by interceding with God on the people's behalf, the narrative presents Aaron as morally complicit in the sin, not as a righteous leader standing against wrongdoing.
